answers.question: What's it for?
answers.answer: Just for me, to show friends

answers.question: What should it have?
answers.answer: My name, a few things I like, a photo spot

title: A page about me
summary: You'll build a friendly one-page website that shows your name, a round photo spot, and a list of things you like. A little JavaScript adds a button that shows a random fun fact about you.
outcome: A colourful 'about me' page you can open from your project folder and show to friends, with a clickable photo spot and a fun-fact button.
learns: Making a round photo spot with CSS

simpler.title: Just your styled card
simpler.why: Build a simple card about you and give it some colour first, then add the clicky extras later.

files.content:
🙂

Hi, I'm Sam!

Welcome to my little corner of the internet.

Things I like

  • 🎮 Video games
  • 🍕 Pizza on Fridays
  • 🎵 Loud music
  • 🐶 Dogs, all of them
  • ⚽ Playing football

steps.title: Build the page skeleton
steps.instruction: In index.html, type the basic frame every web page needs: the first line that says it's a web page, then an html part holding an empty head part and an empty body part.
steps.why: Every web page starts with this frame, so the browser knows what it's reading.

checks.say: I can't see the frame of your page yet.
Something in your page frame looks unfinished. Check every opening tag has its closing partner.

hints: A page has a hidden part with information (the head) and a visible part (the body), both wrapped inside one big part.
Start with <!DOCTYPE html>, then open <html lang="en">. Inside it, put <head></head> and then <body></body>.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
</head>
<body>
…
</html>

concept.title: Tags
concept.explain: HTML uses tags in angle brackets, like <body>, and most come in pairs: one opens, one with a slash closes.

steps.title: Fill in the head
steps.instruction: Inside the head part, add four lines: one for the letter set (UTF-8), one so the page fits phone screens, a title that says About Me, and a link to a file called style.css.
steps.why: This gives your tab a name and connects the page to the styling file you'll write later.
steps.expected:
<meta charset="UTF-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
  <title>About Me</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">

checks.say: Your page doesn't have a tab title yet.
Your page isn't connected to the style file yet.
checks.name: href

checks.say: I can't find the line that sets the letters to UTF-8.
checks.name: charset

checks.say: I can't find the line that helps your page fit phone screens.

hints: The head holds information about the page that doesn't show up in the page itself.
Between <head> and </head>, add two <meta> lines, a <title>, and a <link> pointing to style.css.

<meta charset="UTF-8">
<meta name="viewport" content="…">
<title>…</title>
<link rel="stylesheet" href="…">

concept.title: The head
concept.explain: The head holds behind-the-scenes info, like the tab's name and which style file to use.

steps.title: Make your card
steps.instruction: Inside the body, add a main part with the class card. Inside it, put a box with class photo and id photo holding a 🙂, a big heading saying hi with your name, and a short welcome sentence with class intro.
steps.why: This is the heart of your page: your face, your name and a hello.
steps.expected:

Welcome to my little corner of the internet.

checks.say: I can't see your card with your name in it yet.
I can't find your photo spot yet.
I can't see your welcome sentence yet.

concept.title: Class and id
concept.explain: A class is a name tag you can give many things; an id is a name tag for exactly one thing.

steps.title: List things you like
steps.instruction: Under your welcome sentence, add a smaller heading saying Things I like, then a bullet list with class likes holding 5 things you like.
steps.why: Lists are perfect for showing lots of small things neatly.

anchor.after: Welcome to my little corner of the internet.

steps.expected:
Things I like

  • 🎮 Video games
  • 🍕 Pizza on Fridays
  • 🎵 Loud music
  • 🐶 Dogs, all of them
  • ⚽ Playing football

checks.say: I can't see your list of 5 things you like yet.
Add a small heading above your list saying Things I like.

hints: Give your list a little title first, then write each thing you like as its own bullet.
Use an <h2> for the title, then a <ul class="likes"> with five <li> items inside.

Things I like

  • 🎮 Video games
  • …
    • …

concept.title: Lists
concept.explain: A <ul> is a bullet list, and each <li> inside it is one bullet.

steps.title: Add a button and connect the script
steps.instruction: Under your list, add a button with id fact-button that says Tell me a fun fact, and an empty paragraph with class fact and id fact. Then, just below the closing main tag, add a line that loads script.js.
steps.why: The button and empty spot are ready for the fun facts your code will show later.

checks.say: I can't see your fun fact button yet.
Add an empty paragraph under the button where the fact will appear.
Your page isn't loading the code file yet.
checks.name: src

hints: You need three things: a button, an empty spot for the fact, and a line that loads your code file.
Use
…

concept.title: Buttons
concept.explain: A <button> is something people can click, and later your code decides what happens.

quiz.question: Which tag makes one bullet in a list?
quiz.explain: <li> is one list item; <ul> is the whole list.

steps.title: Look at your plain page
steps.instruction: Open index.html in your browser. Everything is there, but it looks plain. Next you'll add colour!
steps.why: Seeing the plain version shows how much styling changes.
hints: Open your index.html file in a browser.
Double-click index.html or use your editor's preview.
Look at your name, list and button.

steps.title: Colour the background
steps.instruction: In style.css, add a rule for body: no margin, full screen height, everything centred with flex, the Arial font, and a pink-to-purple gradient background.
steps.why: This gives your whole page a colourful background and puts your card in the middle.

checks.say: Your page isn't centred yet.
Your items aren't centred side to side yet.
Something in your style file looks unfinished. Check your curly brackets and semicolons.

hints: Write a rule that says which part to style, then list the looks inside curly brackets.
Start with body { and add margin, min-height, display: flex, justify-content, align-items, font-family and background, each ending with ;.

concept.title: CSS rules
concept.explain: A CSS rule picks part of the page, then lists how it should look inside curly brackets.

steps.title: Style the card
steps.instruction: Under the body rule, add a rule for .card: white background, 320px wide, 30px padding, rounded 20px corners, centred text and a soft shadow.
steps.why: Your content now sits on a neat white card that floats above the background.

checks.say: Your card doesn't have rounded corners yet.
Your card's writing isn't centred yet.

hints: A dot in front of a name styles everything with that class.
Write .card { and add background, width, padding, border-radius, text-align and box-shadow.

concept.title: Styling by class
concept.explain: Putting a dot before a class name, like .card, styles everything wearing that name tag.

steps.title: Make the photo round
steps.instruction: Under the card rule, add a rule for .photo: 120px wide and tall, centred with margin 0 auto, and border-radius 50% to make it a circle.
steps.why: Half-rounded corners on a square turn it into a perfect circle.

checks.say: Your photo spot isn't round yet.
Your photo spot isn't 120px wide yet.

hints: A square with very round corners becomes a circle.
Write .photo { with width and height of 120px, margin: 0 auto, and border-radius: 50%.

concept.title: Rounded corners
concept.explain: border-radius rounds the corners of a box, and 50% makes a square into a circle.

steps.title: Decorate the photo
steps.instruction: Inside the .photo rule, under border-radius, add a gradient background, a 5px purple border, a big 64px emoji, line-height 120px to centre it, and a pointer cursor.
steps.why: Your face circle now looks fun and shows it can be clicked.

checks.say: Your photo doesn't show a hand when you point at it yet.
Your emoji isn't big yet.
Your photo doesn't have a border yet.

hints: Add more looks to the same photo rule, before its closing curly bracket.
Add background, border, font-size, line-height and cursor lines inside .photo.

steps.title: Colour the writing
steps.instruction: Under the .photo rule, add three small rules: a purple colour for h1, grey for .intro, and pink with size 20px for h2.
steps.why: Colourful headings make your page feel friendly.

checks.say: Your name isn't purple yet.
Your small heading isn't pink yet.
Your welcome sentence isn't grey yet.

hints: Make one rule for each kind of writing and give it a colour.
Use h1, .intro and h2 rules, each with a color line. h2 also gets font-size.

concept.title: Colours
concept.explain: Colours can be written as a # followed by six letters and numbers, like #6a4c93 for purple.

steps.title: Style the list
steps.instruction: Under the h2 rule, add a .likes rule that removes the bullets and padding, then a .likes li rule giving each item a light purple background, spacing and rounded corners.
steps.why: Your list turns into neat little bubbles.

checks.say: Your list still has bullet dots.
Your list items don't have rounded corners yet.

hints: First style the whole list, then style each item inside it.
Write .likes { with list-style: none and padding: 0 }, then .likes li { with background, margin, padding and border-radius }.

concept.title: Styling things inside things
concept.explain: Writing .likes li means: style only the list items that sit inside the likes list.

steps.title: Style the button
steps.instruction: Under the list rules, add a button rule: space above, padding, no border, rounded 20px corners, purple background, white 16px text and a pointer cursor.
steps.why: A round colourful button looks inviting to click.

checks.say: Your button isn't purple yet.
Your button's writing isn't white yet.

hints: Give the button a rule of its own and list its looks.
Write button { with margin-top, padding, border, border-radius, background, color, font-size and cursor.

steps.title: Hover colour and fact style
steps.instruction: Under the button rule, add button:hover with a pink background, then a .fact rule with a minimum height of 20px, purple colour and slanted (italic) text.
steps.why: The button changes colour when you point at it, and facts will look special.

checks.say: Your fun fact spot isn't slanted yet.
Your button doesn't change colour when you point at it yet.
checks.question: Is there a button:hover rule that sets a pink background (#ff6f91)?

hints: Adding :hover after a name gives it a look only when the mouse is over it.
Write button:hover { background: … } and then .fact { with min-height, color and font-style }.

concept.title: Hover
concept.explain: :hover gives something a different look only while your mouse is over it.

quiz.question: What does border-radius: 50% do to a square?
quiz.explain: Rounding the corners by half the size makes a perfect circle.

steps.title: Admire your card
steps.instruction: Refresh your page in the browser. Point at the button to see it change colour!
steps.why: You can see all your styling come together.
hints: Refresh the browser tab.
Press F5 or the refresh button.
Hover over the button.

steps.title: Find the parts of your page
steps.instruction: In script.js, make three names: photo, factButton and fact, each finding the matching part of your page by its id.
steps.why: Your code needs a way to reach the photo, button and fact spot before it can change them.

checks.say: Your code isn't finding the photo, button and fact spot yet.
checks.question: Does script.js create constants photo, factButton and fact using document.getElementById with the ids photo, fact-button and fact?

checks.say: Something in your code looks unfinished. Check your brackets and quote marks.

hints: Give each part of the page a name in your code by looking it up with its id.
Use const and document.getElementById("…") three times, for photo, fact-button and fact.

concept.title: Variables
concept.explain: const gives something a name so your code can use it again later.

steps.title: Change faces on click
steps.instruction: Under those three lines, add a list called faces with 5 emojis and a counter faceNumber starting at 0. Then, at the end of the file, make clicking the photo move the counter up, go back to 0 at the end, and show the next face.
steps.why: Now your photo reacts when someone clicks it!

checks.say: Clicking your photo doesn't change the face yet.
checks.question: Does script.js add a click listener to photo that increases faceNumber, resets it to 0 when it reaches faces.length, and sets photo.textContent to faces[faceNumber]?

checks.say: Something in your code looks unfinished. Check your brackets.

hints: Keep a list of faces and a number that remembers which face is showing; on each click, go to the next one.
Use an array in [ ], let faceNumber = 0, then photo.addEventListener("click", function () { … }) with an if to go back to 0.

concept.title: Click events
concept.explain: addEventListener tells the page: when this thing gets clicked, run these lines of code.

steps.title: Write your fun facts
steps.instruction: Under the faceNumber line, add a list called facts holding 5 fun facts about you, each in quotes and separated by commas.
steps.why: These are the facts your button will pick from.
steps.expected:
const facts = [
  "I can eat a whole pizza by myself.",
  "My favourite colour is purple.",
  "I once scored a goal from the halfway line.",
  "I have watched my favourite film ten times.",
  "I want a dog called Biscuit."
];

checks.say: I can't find your list of 5 fun facts yet.
checks.question: Does script.js define a const array named facts containing 5 strings?

checks.say: Something in your list looks off. Check the quotes and commas.

hints: It's a list just like faces, but with sentences instead of emojis.
Use const facts = [ ]; with each fact in quotes and a comma between them.

concept.title: Lists in code
concept.explain: An array is a list in square brackets, and each item has a number starting from 0.

steps.title: Show a random fact
steps.instruction: At the very end of the file, make clicking the button pick a random number up to the number of facts and show that fact in the fact spot.
steps.why: Your button now surprises people with a random fun fact.

checks.say: Clicking your button doesn't show a fun fact yet.
checks.question: Does script.js add a click listener to factButton that picks a random index with Math.floor(Math.random() * facts.length) and sets fact.textContent to that fact?

checks.say: Something in your code looks unfinished. Check your brackets.

hints: It works like the photo click, but picks a random fact instead of the next face.
Use factButton.addEventListener("click", …) and Math.floor(Math.random() * facts.length) to get a random number.

concept.title: Random numbers
concept.explain: Math.random gives a surprise number, and Math.floor rounds it down to a whole number.

quiz.question: What does addEventListener("click", …) do?
options: Runs code when something is clicked
quiz.explain: It waits for a click and then runs the code you gave it.

steps.title: Try it out
steps.instruction: Refresh your page. Click your face to change it, and press the button for fun facts!
steps.why: You built a working interactive page all by yourself.
hints: Refresh the browser tab.
Click the round face a few times.
Press the fun fact button again and again.
